lead: Paul's short blessing for the Thessalonians asks that the whole person be kept ready “at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ”, and adds a promise: “The one who calls you is faithful.” The Gospel tells of ten bridesmaids waiting through the night for the bridegroom, and of the oil that cannot be borrowed at the last moment. The Panchangam also remembers St Catherine of Siena, a woman of prayer whose lamp burned brightly in a dark time. The key words are ready and faithful.

r.h: May the God of peace sanctify you entirely
set: 1 Thessalonians is very probably the oldest writing of the New Testament, sent by Paul from Corinth around AD 50–51 to a young church he had to leave in a hurry (Acts 17:1–10). The readers had questions about the Lord's coming and about members who had died (4:13–5:11). Today's verses are the letter's closing blessing and greetings.
str: v. 23: the prayer: holiness of the whole person until the Lord's coming.
v. 24: the promise: God who calls is faithful.
vv. 25–26: “pray for us”; the holy kiss.
kw: Complete, through and through. Paul prays that no part of life be left outside God's holiness.

Paul is not giving a lesson in how a person is made, but naming the whole human being. The Catechism explains that “spirit” here signifies that man is ordered from his creation to a supernatural end (CCC 367).
The word for the visit of a king. In the New Testament it is the Lord's coming in glory.
vv: May the God of peace himself sanctify you entirely; and may your spirit and soul and body be kept sound and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Holiness reaches the body too. That is why the Church cares for the body: in fasting and feasting, in chastity, in care for the sick, in reverence for the dead.
The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do this.
The whole of Christian hope rests here. We do not make ourselves holy; God who began the work will finish it, if we let him.
Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss.
An early sign of peace among believers. The Church's liturgies kept it in the kiss of peace.
ch: The Catechism takes verse 23 to explain the unity of body and soul: the distinction of soul and spirit does not make two souls in man (CCC 367). Verse 24 grounds the Christian virtue of hope, which rests not on our strength but on God's faithfulness to his promises (CCC 1817). For a West Syriac Christian the holy kiss is familiar: in the Holy Qurbono the peace is passed from the altar to the people at the beginning of the anaphora, as a sign that we come to the offering reconciled.

set: This parable of readiness, spoken on the Mount of Olives, comes straight after yesterday's faithful servant. It reflects a village wedding: the bridegroom came, often at night, to bring the bride to his home, and young women went out with lights to join the procession. The exact customs are not fully known, but the picture was clear to Jesus' hearers. The Old Testament prophets had already called God the bridegroom of his people (Hosea 2:19–20; Isaiah 62:5).
str: vv. 1–4: ten bridesmaids; five take oil, five do not.
vv. 5–7: the delay, the sleep, the midnight shout.
vv. 8–9: the request for oil and the refusal.
vv. 10–12: the door shut; “I do not know you”.
kw: Unmarried young women of the bride's or groom's circle. The NRSV calls them bridesmaids. The Fathers often saw in them the whole Church, waiting for Christ.
Perhaps torches whose rags were soaked in oil, which would burn only a short time without a supply. Hence the need for flasks.
Not “do not sleep”, since all ten slept. It means: be ready, so that when the call comes you can rise and go out.
vv: but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps.
The difference between them is not seen at first. All have lamps, all go out, all sleep. It shows only when the bridegroom comes.
But at midnight there was a shout, ‘Look! Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.’
The hour no one expects. The cry is joyful: the waiting is over.
But the wise replied, ‘No! there will not be enough for you and for us; you had better go to the dealers and buy some for yourselves.’
This is not selfishness. Some things cannot be handed over at the last moment: no one can believe, love or be ready for another.
Keep awake therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
The lesson of the whole discourse in one line.
ch: St Augustine asked what the oil means and answered that it is charity, love that is hidden within and keeps the lamp burning (Sermon 93, in substance). The Catechism quotes the Council's call to watch constantly, since we know neither the day nor the hour, so that we may enter with the Lord into the marriage feast (CCC 1036; Lumen Gentium 48). The parable is serious, but its centre is joy: a bridegroom, a feast, a door opened to those who are ready.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Catherine of Siena (1347–1380), virgin and Doctor of the Church. A laywoman of the Dominican order, she gave herself to prayer and to the sick and poor of her city, and she worked for the return of the Pope from Avignon to Rome and for peace in the Church. Her Dialogue is a classic of Christian prayer. Her life fits today's Gospel: her biographer, Bl. Raymond of Capua, tells of her mystical espousal to Christ, and she kept her lamp burning to the end.
study: What is the “oil” in my lamp, and how do I keep it supplied day by day?
Paul prays for the sanctifying of spirit, soul and body. Which of these do I most neglect in my life with God?
